Science and research.question: When do AI-generated research ideas expand a scientist’s search space, and when do they anchor it to familiar topics?
Does AI raise scientific novelty most in fields with fragmented knowledge, or in fields with mature data infrastructures?
How does a researcher’s experience alter the use and rejection of AI-generated hypotheses?
Which parts of tacit scientific judgment can be translated into AI-readable representations without losing context?
Does assigning AI to hypothesis generation rather than evaluation change the originality of subsequent research?
How can we separate genuine conceptual novelty from lexical novelty in AI-assisted scientific publications?
Does widespread AI use reduce intellectual diversity within a field even as its average output rises?
Which complementarities between domain expertise, data access, and computing capacity determine AI’s scientific returns?
Do shared AI models help peripheral research teams enter frontier fields or reinforce concentration in leading labs?
How does AI adoption change the division of labor between junior and senior researchers in scientific teams?
Can AI-assisted synthesis bridge distant literatures without erasing disagreements between research traditions?
When do interdisciplinary funding programs generate durable collaborations beyond the grant period?
Does disciplinary distance in a proposal predict scientific breakthroughs differently across funding schemes?
How do mission-oriented grant calls redirect research agendas compared with investigator-led funding?
Which research funding modes best support exploratory work while maintaining useful industry collaboration?
Do industry–science grants change the content of academic research more than its volume?
How do contractual rules on disclosure shape the timing and openness of university–industry knowledge flows?
When does collaboration with industry increase scientific reach, and when does it narrow researchers’ questions?
How does decentralized agenda-setting in science teams affect their ability to pursue unexpected findings?
Which incentives make researchers willing to engage with practitioners without compromising scientific autonomy?
What forms of leadership sustain open scientific collaboration when evidence remains highly uncertain?
Can algorithmic coordination improve citizen-science discovery without privileging already active contributors?
How does access to shared research infrastructure affect which institutions participate in AI-enabled science?
When does national research autonomy protect scientific capacity, and when does it isolate researchers from knowledge flows?
How do geopolitical disruptions alter collaboration networks in science differently from those in technology?
Which indicators distinguish AI’s contribution to knowledge creation from faster production of routine papers?
Are AI methods evaluated differently from conventional methods in entrepreneurship and innovation research?
How does the framing of a research problem determine whether AI aids exploration or merely speeds up solution search?
Do AI tools shift researchers toward questions with readily available data at the expense of important unmeasured problems?
What happens to scientific quality when funding agencies reward cross-disciplinary combinations but teams lack integrative capacity?

Innovation and firms.question: When does AI allow firms to recombine technologically distant knowledge without eroding their existing expertise?
Do AI-enabled recombinations generate genuinely new applications or mainly new combinations of established components?
Which complementary assets let firms turn cumulative AI research into applications across multiple markets?
How do academic founders choose market scope when digital technologies lower downstream entry costs?
Do general-purpose AI capabilities favor broad startups, while specialized data and distribution favor incumbents?
How does managerial expertise change when AI is deployed in innovation-oriented rather than routine operations?
Can small firms adopt AI productively without first building internal data and knowledge-management capabilities?
Does AI adoption widen or narrow innovation gaps between small firms with different knowledge bases?
How does human–AI coordination across tacit and codified knowledge affect the viability of new products?
Which kinds of strategic decisions improve when AI agents simulate rival responses rather than forecast outcomes alone?
Do algorithmic recommendations on digital platforms redistribute discovery toward niche complementors or reinforce winners?
When does a platform rival’s entry induce complementors to diversify across platforms rather than specialize?
How do firms identify unmet uses for existing technologies before a clear market has formed?
Can academic directors help firms identify science-based breakthroughs without narrowing their search to familiar disciplines?
Which signals of scientific commercial potential are useful before patents, licensing, or venture funding appear?
How do science and cluster policies interact in generating high-tech startups across regions?
Do technologically complex regions create more frontier ventures, or merely attract entrepreneurs already equipped to launch them?
Which network behaviors turn entrepreneurial ecosystems’ resources into productive ventures rather than local buzz?
How do ecosystem configurations shape the survival and scaling of deep-tech firms beyond initial entry?
When does technological novelty attract resources after venture failure, and when does it damage credibility?
How do visual AI measures change what entrepreneurship researchers can infer about founder teams and venture contexts?
Does the use of AI methods in venture evaluation reduce perceived credibility even when predictive performance improves?
How does access to compute alter the boundary between upstream AI infrastructure firms and downstream application startups?
What determines whether a university spin-off can turn exploratory research into an investable product strategy?
Which forms of industry–university collaboration help smaller firms absorb scientific knowledge rather than outsource R&D?
How do supply-chain ties and skill-related suppliers affect firms’ capacity to enter new technological activities?
Do firms gain more from AI when they use it to search across technologies or to deepen established trajectories?
When do environmental regulations encourage growth-oriented startups to adopt substantive green practices rather than symbolic ones?
How can the impact of sustainable startups be measured beyond venture growth and self-reported intentions?
Which business models let young firms coordinate complementary actors in disruptive sustainability transitions?

Regions and policy.question: How do carbon markets affect the direction of regional green innovation, beyond the number of green patents?
Do market-based environmental policies foster more radical clean technologies than prescriptive rules, and where?
When do public procurement and voluntary standards complement each other in creating markets for green products?
Which regional capabilities allow climate policy to induce innovation rather than relocation of inventive activity?
How should innovation policy account for environmental harms that arise far from the places where technologies are developed?
Can regions identify harmful or foregone innovations before their costs become visible in market data?
How do technical standards redistribute value between regions that develop technologies and those that implement them?
Which actors set AI and green-technology standards, and how does their geography shape entry opportunities?
Does control of standard-essential patents create new regional specializations or deepen existing technological hierarchies?
When can latecomer regions influence international standards instead of remaining standard takers?
How does state participation in global production networks reshape the location of research and strategic assets?
Do technology-sovereignty policies build domestic capabilities or fragment international knowledge exchange?
How can mission-oriented policy coordinate firms and researchers without locking in one technological solution?
At what stage do technology-deployment subsidies begin to impede rather than accelerate further innovation?
Which policy mixes support a transition from early experimentation to large-scale deployment without entrenching incumbents?
What counts as success for transformative innovation policy when societal goals conflict across places?
How do publicly funded collaborations balance open research with firms’ incentives to protect intellectual property?
Do regional science investments generate local entrepreneurship or primarily benefit firms elsewhere?
Which kinds of interregional ties help places enter technological fields beyond their existing knowledge base?
Can academic inventors reduce the constraining effect of regional technological relatedness on diversification?
When do multinational subsidiaries create local knowledge spillovers, and when do they extract regional capabilities?
How does the spatial distribution of data and compute infrastructure alter opportunities for regional AI innovation?
Are place-based innovation policies more effective when they target missing capabilities or connect firms to distant ones?
Do green transitions diversify peripheral regions or concentrate advanced activity in established hubs?
How do skill-related supplier networks shape the co-location of innovative firms across regions?
What regional indicators capture the social value of innovation when patenting and productivity miss adverse effects?
Can sustainable entrepreneurship measurably change environmental outcomes at the regional scale?
How do geopolitical shocks affect international scientific cooperation differently from cross-border R&D investment?
When do research-security restrictions preserve strategic capacity, and when do they undermine scientific discovery?
What would an equitable geography of AI-enabled innovation require from funding, standards, and public infrastructure?
